newsitem.title: ZAIRE: U.S. envoy says Zaire peace talks on Friday.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy says Zaire peace talks on Friday.

text.p: U.S. envoy Bill Richardson said on Wednesday Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko and rebel leader Laurent Kabila would hold their first face-to-face meeting on Friday on a South African navy ship in the Atlantic.

"The meeting will take place on Friday on a South African ship. The ship will be sailing from Libreville into international waters," Richardson said after one hour and 40 minutes of talks with Mobutu.
"Hopefully it will lead to peace in Zaire," the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations told reporters in Kinshasa after shuttling between Mobutu and Kabila since Tuesday.
It would be the first direct meeting between the ailing Zairean president and Kabila, whose rebels have seized more than half of Zaire since October and are advancing on Kinshasa.

Richardson was flanked by Zairean Foreign Minister Kamanda wa Kamanda. Mobutu, looking gaunt and thin, stood behind him briefly in the doorway of the presidential villa in the heavily guarded Tshatshi military camp on the banks of the Zaire river.
He said that several African leaders and joint U.N. and Organisation of African Unity envoy Mohamed Sahnoun would be present on the South African ship for the talks on Friday.
Asked what caused Mobutu's change of heart on venue from Gabon, which Kabila rejected on security grounds, Kamanda said: "It was a perception of the higher interest of the nation."

"I want to commend the statesmanlike action of President Mobutu and Mr Kabila in accepting these talks," said Richardson, adding Mobutu gave him a letter to U.S. President Bill Clinton in response to one he had delivered on Tuesday.
"It is our hope there will be a ceasefire while these talks take place," Richardson said. But he added this was a step-by -step process. Kabila has ruled out a ceasefire before talks.
The meeting is expected to take place on the supply ship SAS Outeniqua, which is already waiting off the coast of Zaire, and was to be chaired by South African President Nelson Mandela.
Richardson said part of the agreement was that he should attend the beginning of the talks and added in the next two days he might go on to South Africa, Gabon and possibly Angola.
Asked what the agenda for the talks was, Richardson said that would be discussed at the encounter. Kabila has said he wanted only a brief meeting to discuss Mobutu's stepping down.
Asked if there were any preconditions for the talks, the U.S. envoy said: "There are no preconditions for the talks."
What made Mobutu change his mind? Richardson replied: "I believe because of a view that there had to be unity and a lack of discord in the country."
He said the talks would be under U.N. auspices but said the United States "was proud to have played this catalyst role".
Earlier on Wednesday, Kabila appealed to the international community to force Mobutu to attend talks at sea to avoid a battle for Kinshasa, the teeming capital of five million people.

A diplomat travelling with Richardson said on Tuesday that Mobutu, who had prostate cancer surgery in Europe in August and met the envoy on Tuesday, turned down the South African offer to host the talks at sea.
South African Deputy Foreign Minister Pahad said the naval vessel was a compromise venue close to Zaire where Mobutu and Kabila, suspicious of each other, could be assured of safety.
Before the meeting was announced, an airlift home of Rwandan refugees from rebel-held Zaire got off the ground on Wednesday but hit problems when a fuel shortage grounded more than two flights.

The U.N. refugee agency UNHCR said 186 unaccompanied refugee children left Kisangani's international airport for Rwanda's capital on an Ilyushin plane and 50 more refugees flew out on another aircraft.
On a brief visit to Kisangani before flying to Kinshasa on Wednesday, Richardson had stormed into a crowd of Rwandan Hutu refugees in Zaire on Wednesday all smiles and handshakes.
He stopped in front of a young Hutu woman and gently stroked the brow of the child she was carrying.
"She's cold," Richardson said. "She's dead," the mother said.
"I'm sorry," Richardson said, "I'm so sorry," and his mood appeared to sink as he continued with his tour of Kisangani.
Richardson questioned the human rights record of the rebels and said the world wanted an investigation of allegations of a massacre of refugees by Zairean villagers and rebels last week.
